cues.text: A Bishop Eager for Reform
Scipione de' Ricci was appointed Bishop of Pistoia and Prato in 1780, with the encouragement of Pope Pius VI himself.
He pursued a program of diocesan reform genuinely concerned, in significant part, with his people's moral improvement and better formation of his clergy.
Over the following years, however, his reforming zeal absorbed increasingly strong currents of Jansenism , Gallicanism , and Richerism.
These movements were then circulating among French appellant theologians and, in different ways, sought to limit papal authority and reshape traditional Catholic devotional and sacramental practice.
Ducal Pressure for Reform
Ricci's diocesan program aligned closely with the ecclesiastical policy of Grand Duke Leopold of Tuscany , brother of Emperor Joseph II.
Leopold circulated fifty-seven proposed reform articles to his territory's bishops and directed diocesan synods to consider them.
Only three of Tuscany's eighteen bishops actually took up the directive, with Ricci proving by far the most enthusiastic and thoroughgoing of the three.
Eighty-Five Propositions
Meeting at Pistoia in September 1786, the synod was assisted by specially invited theologians and canonists known for Jansenist and Gallican sympathies.
It adopted decrees touching on the Mass, clerical authority, popular devotions, and the structure of Church governance.

These provisions discouraged devotion to the Sacred Heart and veneration of relics and images, questioned traditional teaching on indulgences, and proposed sweeping liturgical changes, including celebrating Mass with a single altar per church and greater use of the vernacular.
Rejected Even in Tuscany
When Leopold convened the bishops of the whole Grand Duchy at Florence in 1787, he hoped to secure wider acceptance of the Pistorian program.
After nineteen contentious sessions, the assembled prelates rejected it decisively, forcing Leopold to abandon the project entirely.
Ricci himself grew increasingly isolated and, following Leopold's accession to the imperial throne in 1790, was compelled to resign his see.
Legacy
Pope Pius VI examined the synod's acts through a commission of bishops and theologians.
In the bull Auctorem Fidei of August 28, 1794, he formally catalogued and condemned eighty-five propositions drawn directly from Pistoia's own decrees as erroneous, dangerous, or worse.
This was one of the most detailed doctrinal censures any regional synod has ever received from Rome.
Ricci himself submitted after the bull's publication and, in 1805, personally sought and received reconciliation from Pope Pius VII.
Pistoia remains, in retrospect, a preview of debates over liturgy, clerical authority, and the proper limits of local ecclesiastical reform.
The Catholic Church would revisit those debates, in strikingly different form and with a very different outcome, nearly two centuries later.
